512.title: About my Father's business (Luke 2:41–52)
512.hook: he grew in wisdom and stature and in favor with God and people
512.howItsDone: Many Christians read Luke 2:52 as a picture of whole-person growth, and the finding in the temple is remembered as one of the five Joyful Mysteries of the Catholic rosary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anna, the widowed prophetess praying in the temple night and day. Your line was she never stopped. Did you thank an older woman whose faith kept going? Day five hundred twelve.

A whole day's walk out of Jerusalem, Mary and Joseph realize their son isn't in the crowd. They'd assumed he was with the cousins. Families traveled home from the Passover in big groups, villages walking together, kids running between campfires. So nobody worried, until evening, when they asked around and nobody had seen him. Every parent knows the feeling: the sudden cold drop in the stomach at a mall or a beach. Mary and Joseph turn around and walk back. They search the city. One day. Two days. On the third day they find him, and it's the only story the four Gospels tell about Jesus between his infancy and the day he's grown.
screen: `A DAY'S WALK, AND HE'S NOT THERE.`

segments.voice: Where is he? In the King James Bible, "after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. And notice the order: hearing first, then asking. A twelve-year-old, listening, then asking good questions. Mary says what any mother would: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." And he answers with the first words Luke ever gives him: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" The Greek is shorter than the English. Literally it says something like in the things of my Father, and many translators read it as in my Father's house. Either way, he's naming God as Father, while Joseph stands right there. Luke adds, honestly, that his parents didn't understand. And then he goes home with them to Nazareth, and he obeys them. The boy who knew whose house he was in still goes back to a carpenter's household and does his chores. Then the verse that closes the chapter: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." Increased. Christians believe Jesus was the Son of God, and Luke still says he grew: in learning, in height, in the trust of the people around him. Growth isn't something that happened to him by mistake. Luke writes it down as part of the story. Mary, meanwhile, "kept all these sayings in her heart." She didn't understand yet. She kept it anyway.
screen: then, large: `JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grow a little in one area. Settle, and breathe. Picture the boy in the temple, sitting among people who knew more than he did, listening. Now think of four directions you could grow, the four in Luke's verse. Wisdom: something you want to understand better. Stature: your body, your strength, your sleep. Favor with God: your prayer, or your quiet, or your sense of meaning. Favor with people: one relationship that could be kinder. Let one of the four rise to the top. Then pick the smallest possible step in it: one question to ask someone who knows, one walk, one honest conversation. If you pray, you can ask to grow the way Luke says Jesus grew. If you don't, simply choose your step. The bell holds the time.
About my Father's business. The first words Luke gives Jesus, at twelve, found in the temple after three days, listening and asking, before going home to grow.
Your line: growing is holy. Today, take the one small step you chose, and when you feel slow or behind, remember that even Luke's Jesus increased a little at a time. Day five hundred twelve.

what it means: Jesus' first words in Luke name God as his Father, and then Luke says plainly that he grew in wisdom, stature and favor.

513.title: What shall we do? (Luke 3:1–14)
513.hook: John tells the crowds: share your coat, don't cheat, don't extort
513.howItsDone: Many churches read John the Baptist's preaching during Advent, and Christian charities often take Luke 3:11 as a reason for coat drives and clothing closets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a twelve-year-old in the temple, about my Father's business, and then home to grow. Your line was growing is holy. Did you take your one small step? Day five hundred thirteen.

Luke opens this chapter like a news anchor reading the date. The fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governing Judea. Herod ruling Galilee. His brother Philip, another ruler named Lysanias, the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Seven powerful names, one after another, the people with palaces and armies and seals. And then the sentence lands somewhere else entirely: "the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness." Not to the emperor. Not to the palace. To the son of an old priest, out in the empty country by the Jordan. And the crowds start walking out to hear him.
screen: `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: John doesn't flatter them. He greets them: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" He tells them not to lean on their family tree, and he says the axe is already at the root of the trees. Then he says: "Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." Repentance in Greek is metanoia, a change of mind, a turning around. And the crowd asks the obvious, honest question: "What shall we do then?" Here's what's surprising. John doesn't tell them to move to the desert, or to fast, or to wear camel hair like him. His answers are almost ordinary. To everyone: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." The coat is a tunic, the basic garment worn next to the skin. If you have a spare, someone else is cold. Then the tax collectors come, the people everybody resents, and ask: "Master, what shall we do?" He doesn't tell them to quit. He says: "Exact no more than that which is appointed you." Collect what's owed. Don't pad the bill. Then soldiers come, men with weapons and power over civilians: "And what shall we do?" "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Three groups, three questions, three answers, and each one fits the person's actual job. In Luke, turning around doesn't start in a temple or a monastery. It starts at the closet, the tax booth and the checkpoint. It starts at your own counter, with your own receipts.
screen: then, large: `WHAT SHALL WE DO THEN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do the fair thing in one transaction. Settle, and breathe. Ask John's question about your own work and your own spending: what shall I do? Let your mind walk through a normal week. Where does money or time change hands? A bill you send. A tip you leave. Hours you log. A review you write. A price you set. A favor someone did that you never paid back. Somewhere in there is a small place where you could be a little more honest or a little more generous than you need to be. Let it come up. Don't make it dramatic. John didn't. If you pray, you can ask the crowd's question and listen. If you don't, simply name the one transaction. The bell holds the time.
What shall we do? The question the crowds, the tax collectors and the soldiers all ask John, and his plain, practical answers for each one.
Your line: share your coat. Today, give away one thing you have two of, or make one transaction a little fairer than it has to be. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:15–38)
514.hook: after the baptism, Luke traces Jesus back past Abraham, to Adam, son of God
514.carry: son of adam, son of god
514.howItsDone: Many churches read Luke's account of the baptism on the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, and Christians often point to Luke's genealogy as a sign that Jesus belongs to the whole human family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crowds at the Jordan asking John what shall we do, and his answer: share your coat. Did one thing you had two of find a new home? Day five hundred fourteen.

Most family trees start at the top, with a great-great-grandfather in a faded photograph, and work down to you. Luke does it the other way. He starts with Jesus, about thirty years old, and climbs. Son of Joseph, as people supposed. Son of Heli. Son of Matthat. Back through King David, back through Abraham, back past the flood to Noah, and still he keeps going. More than seventy names, a long ladder of fathers most readers skip. But it's worth reading to the very last rung, because of where Luke puts this list, and because of the strange, beautiful word he ends it on.

First, the setting. People are wondering if John might be the Christ, and he says no: "I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose." Then Jesus is baptized, and Luke adds a detail only he gives: Jesus was praying. "The heaven was opened, And the Holy Ghost descended in a bodily shape like a dove upon him, and a voice came from heaven, which said, Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased." The voice has just said: my Son. And right there, before anything else happens, Luke drops in the genealogy. Matthew's Gospel has one too, but it begins with Abraham and runs forward, a story of Israel's kings. Luke's runs backward and doesn't stop at Abraham. It ends: "Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God." Adam, in Hebrew, simply means human being. So Luke has tied Jesus to every person who has ever lived, not one nation only, but the whole human family. And he's called Adam a son of God too. The voice at the river says this one is my beloved Son, and the list underneath says he belongs to everyone. The two lists don't match name for name between David and Joseph, and Christians have explained that in different ways for a long time: some say Luke follows Mary's family, others say adoption or old family custom explains it. The texts themselves don't say. What Luke does make plain is the shape: from the river all the way back to the garden.
screen: then, large: `WHICH WAS THE SON OF ADAM, WHICH WAS THE SON OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of your grandparents' grandparents. Settle, and breathe. Start with your parents, or whoever raised you. Then their parents. Then one more step back, people you may never have known: names you've heard once, a village, an old photograph, or nothing at all. That's fine. Picture them anyway, eight people, sixteen, people who worked and worried and prayed or didn't, all so that you could be sitting here. Keep going back, past what anyone remembers, until it's just people, the human family Luke traces. If you pray, you can give thanks for the ones whose names are lost. If you don't, simply let yourself feel how long the line is. The bell holds the time.
Son of Adam. Luke climbs Jesus' family tree back past Abraham, to Adam, the human being, and then one more rung, to God.
Your line: son of adam, son of god. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, remember that Luke's list runs through them too, all the way back. Day five hundred fourteen.

515.title: The desert, Luke's way (Luke 4:1–13)
515.hook: full of the Spirit, led into the wilderness, and the devil leaves until an opportune time
515.howItsDone: Many churches read the temptation in the wilderness on the first Sunday of Lent, and the forty days of Lent are often linked to Jesus' forty days in the desert.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's family tree, climbing back to Adam. Your line was son of adam, son of god. Did it change how you saw someone who annoyed you? Day five hundred fifteen.

Anyone who has quit something knows the dangerous moment isn't always the first day. It's day forty. You've made it. You're proud. You're tired. And then the old thing shows up, sounding perfectly reasonable. Luke's story of Jesus in the wilderness begins with a phrase worth noticing. In the King James Bible: "Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness." Full of the Spirit, and led straight into the hardest place. Forty days without food. And Luke says, with almost comic plainness, "when they were ended, he afterward hungered." That's when the voice arrives.
screen: `FULL OF THE SPIRIT, LED INTO THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: The devil makes three offers, and each one is aimed at something real. First, hunger: "If thou be the Son of God, command this stone that it be made bread." Jesus answers from Deuteronomy: "It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." Second, power: all the kingdoms of the world, shown in a moment, if he will only worship. He refuses. Third, Luke takes him to Jerusalem, to a high point of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. And this time the devil quotes scripture too, a psalm about angels bearing you up. Jesus answers: "It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Here's Luke's way. Matthew tells the same three tests, but puts the mountain last. Luke puts Jerusalem last. That's no accident: Luke's whole Gospel walks toward Jerusalem. It opened there, with Zechariah in the temple, and it will end there. And then the line that gives today its name. "And when the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season." The Greek is achri kairou, until an opportune time, until the right moment comes around again. Not gone forever. Just waiting. Luke doesn't pretend the desert was the last test. Readers often see the opportune time return near the end of the Gospel, when Luke says Satan entered into Judas, and in the garden, where Jesus prays in agony. Christians have long read this as honest news: passing one test doesn't end the testing. Temptation keeps a calendar.
screen: then, large: `HE DEPARTED FROM HIM FOR A SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know your weakest hour. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has one. Late at night with the phone. Right after a hard meeting. Sunday evening. The first hour home. Hungry, tired, alone, bored. Walk through an ordinary day in your mind and notice where you tend to slide into the thing you wish you didn't do. Don't scold yourself. Just find the hour, the way you'd find a weak board in a floor. Then think of one small thing to put there ahead of time: a glass of water, a walk, a verse, a friend to text, the phone in another room. If you pray, you can name that hour to God. If you don't, simply name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The desert. In Luke, Jesus goes in full of the Spirit, answers three tests with scripture, and the devil leaves only until an opportune time.
Your line: until another time. Today, when your weakest hour comes around, have the small thing ready, and notice that you saw it coming. Day five hundred fifteen.

516.title: The Nazareth manifesto (Luke 4:14–21)
516.hook: he unrolls Isaiah: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed
516.tomorrow: to the edge of the cliff
516.howItsDone: Many Christian groups working with the poor, prisoners and the sick point to Luke 4:18–19 as their charter, and the passage is read in many churches in the season after Epiphany.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert, and the devil leaving until an opportune time. Your line was until another time. Did your weakest hour show up, and were you ready? Day five hundred sixteen.

A small-town synagogue on a Saturday morning. Wooden benches, maybe stone. Everyone knows everyone. And today the young man who grew up down the street, the carpenter's son, is back home, and word has spread about him. Luke says he went to the synagogue on the sabbath, "as his custom was," a man with a habit of showing up. He stands up to read. The attendant hands him a scroll, the prophet Isaiah. And here's a detail Luke slows down for: he unrolls it, looking for a particular place. He's choosing his words. Whatever he reads next is his first public statement in Luke's Gospel.

He reads, in the King James words: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord." Count who's in it. The poor. The brokenhearted. The captives. The blind. The bruised, the crushed and oppressed. Five kinds of people, and not one of them powerful. That's why readers call this the Nazareth manifesto: a mission statement, read out at the start. The acceptable year of the Lord likely echoes the jubilee in Leviticus, the fiftieth year when debts were released and land returned to families. Then Luke slows everything down: "And he closed the book, and he gave it again to the minister, and sat down. And the eyes of all them that were in the synagogue were fastened on him." Sitting was the teacher's posture. Everyone waits. And then one sentence: "This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears." This day. The Greek word is semeron, today, and it's one of Luke's favorite words. The angels told the shepherds: unto you is born this day. Near the end, on the cross, Jesus will tell a dying man: today thou shalt be with me. In Luke, good news doesn't wait for someday. And there's a quiet detail scholars notice: Jesus stops reading mid-sentence, just before Isaiah's next line about a day of vengeance. Christians read that pause in different ways, but it's there.
screen: `THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.`
`HE SAT DOWN; EVERY EYE ON HIM.`
then, large: `THIS DAY IS THIS SCRIPTURE FULFILLED IN YOUR EARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one of the five to act on. Settle, and breathe. Let the list come back slowly, one at a time, and wait a breath with each. The poor: someone short of money. The brokenhearted: someone grieving or lonely. The captive: someone stuck, in debt, in prison, in a habit. The blind: someone who can't see a way forward. The bruised: someone pushed down by others. One of these will have a face. Let it be someone you actually know, or someone you pass every week. Then choose one small thing you can do for them today, not someday. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
The Nazareth manifesto. Jesus reads Isaiah in his hometown synagogue, good news for the poor, the brokenhearted, the captive, the blind and the bruised, and says: today.
Your line: today this is fulfilled. Do your one small thing for your one person before the sun goes down, and let it be today's, not someday's. Day five hundred sixteen.

517.title: To the edge of the cliff (Luke 4:22–30)
517.word: To the edge of the cliff
517.hook: his own town loves him, then tries to throw him off a cliff, and he walks through them
517.howItsDone: Christians often read the rejection at Nazareth as a picture of how hard it is to hear a prophet close to home, and Nazareth has a traditional hilltop site linked to the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nazareth manifesto, Isaiah's scroll and one word: today. Your line was today this is fulfilled. Did your one small thing happen before sundown? Day five hundred seventeen.

"Is not this Joseph's son?" It's said in the same synagogue, a minute after the reading, and at first it sounds proud. Luke says they "wondered at the gracious words which proceeded out of his mouth." The hometown boy, all grown up. You can almost hear the aunties. But hometowns are complicated. The same people who love you also think they know exactly who you are, and exactly what you owe them. We've heard what you did in Capernaum, they're thinking. Do it here. Within a few verses, this warm room will become a crowd marching him to the edge of a hill.

Jesus names what they're thinking before they say it: "Ye will surely say unto me this proverb, Physician, heal thyself." Then: "Verily I say unto you, No prophet is accepted in his own country." And he reaches for two stories from their own scriptures, stories they knew by heart. In the days of Elijah there was a famine, and many widows in Israel. But the prophet was sent to a widow in Sarepta, in the region of Sidon, outside Israel. In the days of Elisha there were many lepers in Israel, "and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian." A foreign widow. A foreign general. Both from Israel's own prophets, both showing God's care reaching past the expected circle. That's the line that turns the room. Luke says "all they in the synagogue, when they heard these things, were filled with wrath," and the scene moves fast: they "thrust him out of the city, and led him unto the brow of the hill whereon their city was built, that they might cast him down headlong." This isn't a story about one town being worse than others. It's about something every group does: we love the prophet until the prophet says God's kindness isn't only ours. And then the ending, so quiet you can miss it: "But he passing through the midst of them went his way." No miracle is described. No fight, no speech, no running. He just walks through the crowd and keeps going. Luke doesn't explain how. The text is silent, and the silence is part of the picture: the anger doesn't get to decide his direction.
screen: `A WIDOW IN SIDON, A SYRIAN GENERAL.`
`FILLED WITH WRATH, TO THE BROW OF THE HILL.`
`THROUGH THE MIDST, AND ON HIS WAY.`
then, large: `HE PASSING THROUGH THE MIDST OF THEM WENT HIS WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay calm when praise turns. Settle, and breathe. Remember a time when people who liked you suddenly didn't: a group chat that went cold, a family dinner that soured, a boss whose praise flipped into blame. Feel it in your body for a moment, the heat in the chest, the urge to argue or to win them back. Now picture Jesus at the edge of the hill, and the small, steady way he walks through. No shouting. No pleading. Breathe slowly, and let your shoulders drop. Imagine yourself doing the same: not fighting the crowd, not obeying it, just going your way. If you pray, you can ask for that steadiness. If you don't, simply practice the slow breath. The bell holds the time.
To the edge of the cliff. His hometown wonders at him, then turns on him and takes him to a hilltop, and he walks through the middle of them and goes on.
screen: `TO THE EDGE OF THE CLIFF — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he went his way. If praise turns to blame today, take one slow breath before answering, and keep walking in the direction you were already going. Day five hundred seventeen.

518.title: Laying on hands (Luke 4:31–44)
518.hook: at sunset they bring the sick, and he lays his hands on every one
518.howItsDone: Many churches lay hands on people in ordination and confirmation, and in prayer for the sick, including the Catholic and Orthodox anointing of the sick and healing prayer in Pentecostal and charismatic churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the edge of the cliff in Nazareth, and a man who walked through the crowd. Your line was he went his way. When praise turned this week, did you keep walking? Day five hundred eighteen.

Capernaum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. It's the sabbath, a day of rest, and a day when you didn't carry loads around town. All afternoon, people with sick relatives have been waiting. Watching the sky. Because the moment the sun goes down, the sabbath is over, and you can pick someone up and carry them. So as the light turns orange over the water, the streets fill. Mats, stretchers, people leaning on cousins' shoulders, children being carried. Everyone heading to the same door, the house of a fisherman named Simon.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE SUN TO GO DOWN.`

segments.voice: The day began in the synagogue, where a man possessed by an unclean spirit cried out, and Jesus said: "Hold thy peace, and come out of him." People were stunned: "What a word is this!" Then he went to Simon's house, where Simon's mother-in-law lay "taken with a great fever." Luke, often remembered as a physician, says Jesus "stood over her, and rebuked the fever; and it left her: and immediately she arose and ministered unto them." She gets up and serves the table. Then sunset, and the verse that gives today its name: "Now when the sun was setting, all they that had any sick with divers diseases brought them unto him; and he laid his hands on every one of them, and healed them." Every one of them. Not a wave from the doorway to the whole crowd. Not a blessing in bulk. One by one, hands on each person, which on a night like that would have taken hours. Laying on hands was an old gesture in Israel's scriptures, for blessing and for setting someone apart. Christians kept it. Today hands are laid on people in ordination, in confirmation in many churches, and in prayer for the sick, from Catholic and Orthodox anointing to Pentecostal healing services. And here's the ending: at dawn, Jesus slips away to a deserted place. The crowds find him and beg him to stay. He says: "I must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also: for therefore am I sent." Full attention to each person at night. And in the morning, the freedom to leave. Both are part of the same love.
screen: `THE FEVER LEFT; SHE ROSE AND SERVED.`
then, large: `HE LAID HIS HANDS ON EVERY ONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay attention to one person fully. Settle, and breathe. Picture that doorway at sunset, the line of people, and one pair of hands, one person at a time. Now bring to mind the people you'll see today. Who usually gets the half of you that's looking at a screen? A child, a partner, a parent on the phone, a coworker, the person at the register. Choose one. Picture giving them all of you for five minutes: eyes up, phone away, listening to the end of their sentences. Let that picture be clear before the bell. If you pray, you can hold that person before God now. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Laying on hands. At sunset in Capernaum, the sick are carried to the door, and Jesus lays his hands on each one, a gesture churches still use for blessing, healing and sending.

Your line: every one of them. Today, give one person your whole attention. And look back at the week: a boy in the temple, a crowd at the river, a desert, a hometown, a doorway at sunset. Day five hundred eighteen, and another week on the path.
